scorecard.rationale: One randomized non-Parkinson trial reports higher stool frequency (p=.0281) and softer stools (p=.04) with added orange pomace versus control, alongside increased gas/bloating and an unavailable separate constipation severity score (NCT02979496). Competing evidence includes a null pomace crossover for primary stool-frequency interaction (PMID36102329, p=.46), sequential null pasteurized orange juice (PMID30638420), an unadjusted older-adult survey (p=.054), uncontrolled multi-component Chagas and trifoliate-orange studies, and a Fox Insight pooled-fruit binary bowel category pointing opposite. No trial tests raw whole orange in Parkinson constipation; the pomace stool-frequency trial retains a minimal_signal against worsening. The new human constipation source concerns a modified multi-herb formula containing dried citrus peel. The synthesis supplies no component-only comparison or frozen raw-orange estimate, and its low-quality studies do not strengthen the existing orange-pomace lean. The c-Rel mouse study uses a separate orange extract odor challenge and compares stool outcomes by genotype and age. Food administration, processing and direct orange-specific attribution are absent. The earlier dietary evidence still controls the weak easing lean. The randomized probiotic comparison includes an orange-flavored powder and a similar-tasting placebo. The stool-frequency outcome follows probiotic assignment, with no raw-orange group or comparator. The prior orange-pomace direction remains the basis for the weak easing lean. The original Alexander crossover gives inconclusive primary stool-frequency and no-movement-day interactions. Its reported favorable no-movement-day main effect differs between article prose and Table S7, with baseline imbalance. A four-fibre blend improves stool frequency in functional constipation participants without Parkinson disease. These data keep the original weak easing tier for the frozen whole-orange claim.
